title: A MADEMOISELLE
work: Histoires ou contes du temps passé
source: Charles Perrault, « A MADEMOISELLE », dans Histoires ou contes du temps passé. Avec des Moralitez (Paris, Claude Barbin, 1697) ; texte de l’édition originale d’après la transcription de Wikisource, orthographe de 1697 conservée. Prononciation : français standard moderne ; les graphies de 1697 sont lues selon l’usage moderne.
about: This is the dedication that opens Perrault’s book of tales: a letter addressed to Élisabeth-Charlotte d’Orléans, the King’s niece, and signed by Perrault’s teenage son Pierre Darmancour. In ceremonious prose and a few lines of verse it defends offering simple tales to a princess, arguing that a great mind can stoop to small things and that those born to govern should know how humble people live. Who actually wrote the tales, the father or the son, has been argued over ever since.

sentences.n: «Mademoiselle», with no name after it, was a title at the court of Louis XIV and belonged to one person: the eldest unmarried daughter of the King’s brother, known at court simply as «Monsieur». In 1697 that was Élisabeth-Charlotte d’Orléans, the King’s niece, to whom the book is offered. The English keeps the French title, since ‘Miss’ would carry none of its rank; the capitals are the printer’s, the dress of a formal address.

sentences.t: On ne trouvera pas étrange qu’un enfant ait pris plaisir à composer les Contes de ce Recueil ;
sentences.l: One will not find [it] strange that a child has taken pleasure in composing the Tales of this Collection;
sentences.i: No one will think it strange that a child should have enjoyed composing the tales in this collection;
sentences.n: «on» is the indefinite ‘one, people’, and «trouvera» its future, ‘will find’. «ait pris» is the perfect subjunctive of «prendre», which «trouver étrange que» ‘to find it strange that’ calls for; English manages with ‘has’ or ‘should have’. French needs no ‘it’ before «étrange», and the literal line supplies it in brackets. The «enfant» ‘child’ is the letter’s writer speaking of himself; the letter is signed by Perrault’s son Pierre. «Contes» and «Recueil» carry the capitals the 1697 printer gives to many common nouns.

sentences.t: mais on s’étonnera qu’il ait eu la hardiesse de vous les presenter.
sentences.say: mais on s’étonnera qu’il ait eu la hardiesse de vous les présenter.
sentences.l: but one will be astonished that he has had the boldness to present them to you.
sentences.i: but people will be surprised that he has had the boldness to present them to you.
sentences.n: «s’étonner» ‘to astonish oneself’ is ‘to be surprised’, and it too takes the subjunctive («ait eu», from «avoir»). In «vous les presenter» both pronouns stand before the infinitive, ‘you them to present’. «presenter» is printed without the accent of modern «présenter»; accents in 1697 are sparse and irregular. «vous» is the formal address used to the princess throughout.

sentences.t: Cependant, MADEMOISELLE, quelque disproportion qu’il y ait entre la simplicité de ces Recits & les lumieres de votre esprit, si on examine bien ces Contes, on verra que je ne suis pas aussi blamable que je le parois d’abord.
sentences.say: Cependant, MADEMOISELLE, quelque disproportion qu’il y ait entre la simplicité de ces Récits et les lumières de votre esprit, si on examine bien ces Contes, on verra que je ne suis pas aussi blâmable que je le parais d’abord.
sentences.l: However, Mademoiselle, whatever disproportion there may be between the simplicity of these Narratives and the lights of your mind, if one examines these Tales well, one will see that I am not as blameworthy as I appear at first.
sentences.i: And yet, Mademoiselle, however great the distance between the simplicity of these stories and the brilliance of your mind, anyone who looks closely at these tales will see that I am not so much to blame as I seem at first.
sentences.n: «quelque … que» with the subjunctive («ait») is ‘whatever … there may be’. «lumieres» ‘lights’ is the period’s word for understanding and knowledge, the same word that later named the French Enlightenment, and «esprit» here is ‘mind’. «parois» is the 1697 spelling of «parais» ‘I appear’, an «oi» where modern French writes «ai»; its «le» stands for «blamable» (modern «blâmable»), a pronoun French requires and English leaves out. «&» is the printer’s sign for «et» ‘and’.

sentences.t: Ils renferment tous une morale trés-sensée, & qui se découvre plus ou moins, selon le degré de pénetration de ceux qui les lisent ;
sentences.say: Ils renferment tous une morale très-sensée, et qui se découvre plus ou moins, selon le degré de pénétration de ceux qui les lisent ;
sentences.l: They contain, all of them, a very sensible moral, and one which reveals itself more or less, according to the degree of penetration of those who read them;
sentences.i: Every one of them holds a very sensible moral, which shows itself more or less clearly according to the discernment of those who read them;
sentences.n: «renfermer» is ‘to enclose, to hold within’, and «tous» after the verb is ‘all of them’. «trés-sensée» is how 1697 prints «très sensée»: a hyphen binds «très» to its adjective, with an acute accent where modern French has a grave. «& qui» adds a second description to «une morale» as though the first had been a relative clause as well; the literal line gives ‘and one which’. «se découvre» ‘uncovers itself’ is ‘comes to light’, and «pénetration» is keenness of mind.

sentences.t: d’ailleurs, comme rien ne marque tant la vaste estenduë d’un esprit, que de pouvoir s’élever en même temps aux plus grandes choses, & s’abaisser aux plus petites ; on ne sera point surpris que la même Princesse à qui la nature & l’éducation ont rendu familier ce qu’il y a de plus élevé ne dédaigne pas de prendre plaisir à de semblables bagatelles.
sentences.say: d’ailleurs, comme rien ne marque tant la vaste étendue d’un esprit, que de pouvoir s’élever en même temps aux plus grandes choses, et s’abaisser aux plus petites ; on ne sera point surpris que la même Princesse à qui la nature et l’éducation ont rendu familier ce qu’il y a de plus élevé ne dédaigne pas de prendre plaisir à de semblables bagatelles.
sentences.l: besides, as nothing marks so much the vast extent of a mind as to be able to raise itself at the same time to the greatest things, and to lower itself to the smallest; one will not at all be surprised that the same Princess to whom nature and education have made familiar what is most lofty does not disdain to take pleasure in such trifles.
sentences.i: besides, since nothing so shows the breadth of a mind as the power to rise to the greatest things and at the same time to stoop to the smallest, no one will be surprised that the very Princess whom nature and upbringing have made at home with all that is most exalted should not scorn to take pleasure in trifles such as these.
sentences.n: «d’ailleurs» is ‘besides, moreover’. «rien ne marque tant … que de pouvoir» is ‘nothing marks so much … as being able’, and «estenduë» is the 1697 spelling of «étendue» ‘extent, range’, with an «s» where modern French has an accent. The compliment turns on the pair «s’élever» ‘to raise oneself’ and «s’abaisser» ‘to lower oneself’. «ne … point» is a firmer ‘not’. «ne dédaigne pas» is in the subjunctive, which «être surpris que» calls for, though here its form is the same as the present. The semicolon stands where a modern printer would put a comma. «bagatelles» ‘trifles’ is a modest name for the tales.

sentences.t: Il est vray que ces Contes donnent une image de ce qui se passe dans les moindres Familles, où la loüable impatience d’instruire les enfans fait imaginer des Histoires dépourveuës de raison, pour s’accommoder à ces mêmes enfans, qui n’en ont pas encore ;
sentences.say: Il est vrai que ces Contes donnent une image de ce qui se passe dans les moindres Familles, où la louable impatience d’instruire les enfants fait imaginer des Histoires dépourvues de raison, pour s’accommoder à ces mêmes enfants, qui n’en ont pas encore ;
sentences.l: It is true that these Tales give a picture of what goes on in the lowliest Families, where the praiseworthy impatience to instruct the children makes [people] imagine Stories devoid of reason, to suit themselves to those same children, who have none of it yet;
sentences.i: It is true that these tales give a picture of what goes on in the humblest households, where a laudable eagerness to instruct the children leads their elders to invent stories with no reason in them, to suit children who have no reason yet;
sentences.n: «moindres» ‘least’ is ‘humblest, lowliest’, a matter of rank, not size. «fait imaginer» is ‘makes (someone) imagine’: the French does not say who does the imagining, so the literal line supplies ‘people’ in brackets. «en» in «qui n’en ont pas encore» takes up «raison»: the stories lack reason because the children do, and both English lines keep the play on the word. «vray», «loüable», «enfans» and «dépourveuës» are 1697 spellings of «vrai», «louable», «enfants» and «dépourvues».

sentences.t: mais à qui convient-il mieux de connoître comment vivent les Peuples, qu’aux Personnes que le Ciel destine à les conduire ?
sentences.say: mais à qui convient-il mieux de connaître comment vivent les Peuples, qu’aux Personnes que le Ciel destine à les conduire ?
sentences.l: but to whom is it more fitting to know how the Peoples live, than to the Persons whom Heaven destines to lead them?
sentences.i: but whom does it better befit to know how the common people live than those whom Heaven has destined to govern them?
sentences.n: «convenir à» is ‘to befit, to be fitting for’, with the impersonal «il» set after the verb in the question. «les Peuples» here are the common people, those who are governed, not nations. «connoître» is the 1697 spelling of «connaître» ‘to know’, the same «oi» for modern «ai» as in «parois». Heaven’s destining is a compliment to a princess of the royal blood, counted among those born to rule.

sentences.t: Le desir de cette connoissance a poussé des Heros, & même des Heros de vostre Race, jusque dans des huttes & des cabanes, pour y voir de prés, & par eux-mêmes, ce qui s’y passoit de plus particulier, cette connoissance leur ayant paru nécessaire pour leur parfaite instruction.
sentences.say: Le désir de cette connaissance a poussé des Héros, et même des Héros de votre Race, jusque dans des huttes et des cabanes, pour y voir de prés, et par eux-mêmes, ce qui s’y passait de plus particulier, cette connaissance leur ayant paru nécessaire pour leur parfaite instruction.
sentences.l: The desire for this knowledge has driven Heroes, and even Heroes of your Line, right into huts and cabins, to see there close up, and for themselves, what went on there that was most private, this knowledge having seemed to them necessary for their complete instruction.
sentences.i: The desire for such knowledge has led heroes, and even heroes of your own house, into huts and hovels, to see close at hand and with their own eyes the most private details of life there, since they judged this knowledge necessary to complete their education.
sentences.n: «Race» is ‘line, family’, here the royal house of Bourbon from which the princess descends. The letter names no one; it may be thinking of the stories told of kings who went among their poorer subjects, Henri IV above all, but that is only a likely guess. «de plus particulier» is ‘most private, most personal’, and «y» ‘there’ points twice back to the huts. «passoit» is the 1697 spelling of «passait», and «vostre» of «votre», though the same letter also prints «votre»; spellings vary within a single page. «ayant paru» ‘having seemed’ is a participle clause giving the reason.

sentences.i: Be that as it may, Mademoiselle,
sentences.n: «Quoi qu’il en soit» is ‘whatever may be the case’, with «soit», the subjunctive of «estre» ‘to be’. It closes the prose argument and hands over to the verses, which carry on the same address.

sentences.t:
Pouvois-je mieux choisir pour rendre vrai-semblable
Ce que la Fable a d’incroyable ?
sentences.say:
Pouvais-je mieux choisir pour rendre vraisemblable,
Ce que la Fable a d’incroyable ?
sentences.l:
Could I better choose, to render likely
What Fable has that is unbelievable?
sentences.i:
Could I have chosen better, to make plausible
what fable holds that is past belief?
sentences.n: «Pouvois-je» is ‘could I’, the imperfect of «pouvoir» in its 1697 spelling (modern «pouvais-je»), with the subject pronoun after the verb as in any question. «vrai-semblable» ‘true-seeming’ is modern «vraisemblable» ‘likely, plausible’, printed in two halves. «ce que la Fable a d’incroyable» is ‘what fable has of the unbelievable’; «la Fable» means invented stories in general. The compliment the verses build: a princess so richly gifted makes the fairies’ gifts in the tales believable.

sentences.t:
Et jamais Fée, au tems jadis,
Fit-elle à jeune Créature
Plus de dons, & de dons exquis,
Que vous en a fait la Nature ?
sentences.say:
Et jamais Fée, au temps jadis,
Fit-elle à jeune Créature,
Plus de dons, et de dons exquis,
Que vous en a fait la Nature ?
sentences.l:
And ever [a] Fairy, in the time of old,
Did she make to [a] young Creature
More gifts, and gifts exquisite,
Than Nature has made you of them?
sentences.i:
And did any fairy, in the days of old,
ever bestow upon a young creature
more gifts, and exquisite gifts,
than Nature has bestowed on you?
sentences.n: «jamais» without «ne», in a question, is ‘ever’. «Fit-elle» repeats the subject «Fée» as a pronoun after the verb, the formal way of asking a question whose subject is a noun, still usual in written French: ‘ever a Fairy, did she make…?’. «Fit» is the passé simple of «faire», the tense of narrative, of things done and finished in the past; it has left everyday speech, and English renders it with its plain past. «faire des dons» ‘to make gifts’ is the phrase the tales use for fairies at a christening. «tems» is an older spelling of «temps» ‘time’, and «jadis» is ‘of old’. The articles are left out before «Fée» and «jeune Créature», as older French often allowed, above all in verse and after «jamais»; the literal line supplies ‘a’ in brackets. «en» in «vous en a fait» stands for the gifts: ‘has made you of them’.

sentences.t: Je suis avec un trés profond respect,
sentences.say: Je suis avec un très profond respect,
sentences.l: I am with a very deep respect,
sentences.i: I am, with the deepest respect,
sentences.n: The closing formula of a formal letter begins here and runs on over the next lines to the signature: ‘I am, with very deep respect, Mademoiselle, of Your Royal Highness the very humble and very obedient servant’. Here «trés» stands apart from «profond», without the hyphen the letter uses in «trés-sensée».
The title returns inside the closing formula, set on a line of its own, as the formal style of a letter to a royal person required.

«Altesse Royale» ‘Royal Highness’ was the style Élisabeth-Charlotte bore as a granddaughter of a king of France, Louis XIII; French puts the adjective after the noun. «Vôtre» is printed with a circumflex that modern French keeps only in «le vôtre» ‘yours’; before a noun it is «votre», as the letter itself prints it earlier. «De» ‘of’ belongs with the line below: ‘of Your Royal Highness the most humble servant’.

sentences.i: most humble and most obedient servant.
sentences.n: «trés-humble» and «trés-obeissant» (modern «très humble», «très obéissant») make up the fixed signing-off of a letter to a superior, the French counterpart of the English ‘most humble and most obedient servant’ of the same age.

«P. Darmancour» is Pierre Perrault Darmancour, Charles Perrault’s son, then not yet twenty, and the royal privilege to print the book was granted in the same name. Whether he wrote the tales, shaped them with his father, or only lent his name to them has been argued over ever since, and the question remains open.
